prize_parts.citation: For experimental realisation of controllable strongly correlated quantum many-body systems with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and quantum gas microscopy

statement.case_for: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned the Hubbard model, a central object of statistical and condensed-matter physics, into a tunable laboratory system. The superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic lattice experiments and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy gave quantitative access to interacting many-body problems that are intractable by analytic or numerical means. The work is conceptually transparent, has been replicated for over twenty years by many independent groups, and has changed how strongly correlated systems are studied, linking AMO physics, condensed matter and quantum information. It is mature, so the interpretation is stable and recognition is timely. Seven of eight members placed it in their top three, which gives me some confidence that it is the least contested choice, though I do not treat that breadth as evidence of merit by itself.
statement.case_against: Five names are credited and only three can be chosen. Choosing the experimental trio leaves out Zoller and Cirac, whose proposals underpin the field, and Jaksch, who is not on the credited list, and the priority between Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger on the first Mott and fermionic results is partly intertwined. There is also overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and recent quantum-technology prizes, and analogue quantum simulation has so far reproduced known physics more than it has solved an open problem such as high-temperature superconductivity.

responses.point: Cirac and Zoller (B011) are the decisive theorists for the ion-trap gate and cold-atom simulation proposals, so the experimental optical-lattice work should be recognised separately and the two candidates should not both reward the same people.
responses.response: I agree that B001 and B011 should not both be prized with the same people, and I agree the experimental trio is the cleaner configuration, which is why I keep Zoller and Cirac out of B001. I qualify the claim that B011 is the stronger standalone case. The ion-trap gate and quantum-simulation proposals are influential, but the physics content that changed my own field, how one studies many-body statistical mechanics, came from the lattice experiments, and a theory-only prize would honour the blueprint without the demonstrations. I would regard B011 as a credible fallback only if the committee prefers theory, but it is not among my two alternatives because B041 and B013 look more distinct.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B041) is the strongest first choice, a rare theory-then-experiment sequence in correlated electrons, with the continuum-model prediction followed by observed correlated insulators and superconductivity.
responses.response: I ranked B041 second and share the admiration for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction as a case of theory preceding experiment. My reservation is maturity: about eight years in, the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states are unsettled, and Eriksson's own concern about omitted first-author experimentalists and the hBN and other experimental groups makes the credited trio harder to defend than the optical-lattice trio. Waiting costs little, since the field is clearly durable, whereas B001 is stable now. I keep B041 as my first alternative and would support it in a later year.

responses.point: The Higgs discovery (B020) is fully mature and still unrecognised on the experimental side, and the founding spokespersons and project leaders can stand for the two collaborations.
responses.response: I agree on importance and maturity, since the discovery is the capstone of the Standard Model. My difficulty is attribution rather than science. Naming spokespersons rewards leadership of thousands of people, and the three-person limit cannot represent two collaborations in a way that identifies who discovered what. The openings also disagree on the names, with Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee each appearing in different trios, which signals that no obvious triple exists. I would support B020 only if the committee can agree on a principled credit rule, and I do not find that case settled.

responses.point: The Higgs discovery should be first and the Bloch-Greiner-Esslinger experimental trio second, with the 2013 prize covering the theory and Zoller's role in the Mott proposal an open allocation question.
responses.response: We agree on the experimental trio for B001, so our disagreement is about ordering. I accept that a prize recognising the LHC discovery would be a landmark, but the attribution problem there is structural, whereas for B001 it is a matter of excluding two excellent theorists. On Zoller I concede the allocation is open, but I think the experiments, not the proposal, are what established the field, so the trio is defensible.

uncertainties: Whether Zoller should replace one experimentalist, as several colleagues propose, or whether the experimental trio is cleaner.
Relative priority among Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger on the first Mott-insulator and fermionic Hubbard results.
Whether the committee judges quantum simulation to have yielded new physics rather than demonstrated capability.
Whether the maturity of B041 will be judged sufficient before a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have not co-authored with any credited candidate, and my own work on turbulence, stochastic processes and neural networks is distant from cold-atom and lattice physics, though statistical-mechanics interest in Hubbard-type models is a shared subject.
